s-wh3_saq1-high-0.essay:
(A) Libby claims that the group that became the Royal Society was an informal circle of scholars who had been meeting in London since about 1645, and they gathered once a week at places like Goddard's house in Wood Street, the Bull's Head Tavern, and Gresham College. He also shows that the members had very different interests, including mathematics, astronomy, navigation and medicine, and that many of them were doctors. This shows the group was organized around a shared curiosity about natural philosophy and not one single field.

(B) One development that helps explain why these scholars met is Francis Bacon's call for an experimental, inductive method in works like the Novum Organum (1620). Bacon argued that knowledge should be built by collecting many observations and testing them through experiments instead of relying on ancient authorities like Aristotle. Since this kind of research needed lots of data and witnesses to check results, scholars had a reason to meet regularly, repeat experiments in front of each other, and share what they observed.

(C) The French Academy of Sciences, founded in 1666 under Louis XIV and his minister Colbert, was different from the London gatherings because it was sponsored and funded by the king. The members were paid by the state and their work was supposed to serve the monarchy's goals, while the London group started as a private, self-organized circle meeting in homes and taverns. This shows that in France science was organized from the top down by an absolutist state, but in England it began from the bottom up among individual scholars.

s-wh3_saq1-mid-0.essay:
(A) Libby claims that the group that became the Royal Society started as an informal circle of men who met about once a week in London starting around 1645, well before it was formally organized in 1662. They met in different places like Goddard's house, a tavern in Cheapside, and Gresham College, and the members had many different interests like mathematics, medicine, and navigation.

(B) One development in Europe in the 1600s was Francis Bacon's idea that people should study nature by doing experiments and collecting observations instead of just relying on old ancient authorities like Aristotle. This made scholars want to work together because one person could not do all the experiments and gather all the facts alone, so meeting to share what they found helped build knowledge.

(C) Another place where science was organized was France, where the Academy of Sciences was set up under Louis XIV. This was different from the London gatherings because it was connected to the government and the king, while the London group started as a private informal group of friends who just met in houses and taverns.

s-wh3_saq1-low-0.essay:
(A) Libby claims that the group that became the Royal Society was made up of men with many different interests who met together in London starting around 1645. He says they met once a week in different places like a house, a tavern and Gresham College, and that they later became the nucleus of the Royal Society when it was organized in 1662.

(B) One development in Europe was the Scientific Revolution, when lots of new ideas about science came up and people got more interested in nature. This made scholars want to meet up and talk about science because science was becoming important in Europe in the 1600s.

(C) In other places like Asia there were also people who studied the stars and nature. They were different from the London group because they did not have the same kind of science as Europe and were not as advanced. Science in Europe was more organized than in other regions.
